title: Musa meets al-Khidr
hook: Musa travels to learn from a servant given knowledge, and promises patience (18:65–70)
carry: you won't be able to be patient
tomorrow: The boat, the boy, the wall

segments.voice: Yesterday, two gardens, and your line was mashallah, no power but His. When you admired something, did you remember whose it was? Day four hundred sixty-eight.

Musa has stood before Pharaoh, crossed the sea, received the Torah. And in a hadith in Bukhari, someone asks him: who is the most knowledgeable person on earth? He says: I am. God corrects him. There is a servant of Mine, at the place where the two seas meet, who knows more than you. So the great teacher packs a bag and goes looking for a teacher, one who will not let him ask questions.
screen: `THE TEACHER GOES LOOKING FOR A TEACHER.`

segments.voice: In the hadith, God tells Musa to carry a fish in a basket: where you lose the fish, you'll find him. Musa sets out with a young servant, named Yusha' in the hadith. At a rock by the sea they rest, and the fish slips into the water and swims off, leaving a strange tunnel in the sea. The young man forgets to mention it. Later, tired and hungry, Musa asks for their meal, and the young man remembers. Musa says: that's the place we were looking for. They retrace their steps. And there, the Qur'an says, they find one of Our servants, to whom We had given mercy from Us and taught knowledge from Our presence. The Qur'an never names him. The hadith calls him al-Khidr, the green one, because, it says, where he sat on bare ground, it turned green. Musa asks, very politely: may I follow you, so that you teach me some of the right guidance you've been taught? And the answer, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! thou canst not bear with me." Then: how could you be patient with what you can't fully understand? Look at Musa's reply. He says, in sha' Allah, you will find me patient, and I won't disobey you in anything. This week's two words, inshallah and mashallah, are still in the air. Al-Khidr sets one condition: if you follow me, don't ask me about anything until I bring it up myself. Musa, a prophet who spoke with God, agrees to be a student who keeps quiet. That's the lesson before any of the lessons. The man who answered I am, when asked who knew the most, still had something to learn, and he was willing to walk to find it.
screen: `A FISH IN A BASKET.` · `THE PLACE WHERE THE SEAS MEET.` · `A SERVANT, UNNAMED: AL-KHIDR.` · `ONE CONDITION: DON'T ASK YET.` · then, large: `LO! THOU CANST NOT BEAR WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you don't usually learn from. Someone younger, or with less schooling, or from a job you overlook, or someone you disagree with. Picture them clearly. Now ask: what do they know that I don't? Maybe how to fix something, how to be calm, how to live on less. Let the answer come slowly. Then imagine yourself asking them about it, and, like Musa, keeping quiet long enough to actually hear the answer. The bell holds the time.
Al-Khidr. The servant of God that Musa traveled to learn from, patient with knowledge Musa was told he couldn't bear. Today's word.
Your line: you won't be able to be patient. Today, learn one thing from someone unexpected, and let them finish before you ask your questions. Day four hundred sixty-eight.

screen: `DAY 468 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BOAT, THE BOY, THE WALL.`

howItsDone: Muslim teachers use the story of Musa and al-Khidr to teach the manners of learning: humility before a teacher, patience, and not presuming one knows the most; it is read with all of al-Kahf on Fridays.

original.note: Arabic: al-Khidr, the green one; the name given in hadith to the servant Musa met (also said al-Khidr or al-Khadir).

trapdoor: what you thought: Musa met a wise man.
what it means: a prophet who claimed to know most is sent to learn, and the first test is to stay quiet.

what a scholar hears: Bukhari's report from Ubayy ibn Ka'b supplies the backstory; scholars debate whether al-Khidr was a prophet or a righteous servant, and the meaning of 'knowledge from Our presence' ('ilm ladunni).
